name: Freya Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a bank of six weaving looms at a textile mill that makes heavy cloth for furniture upholstery. I load the yarn beams, watch for broken threads, tie them back in, and check the cloth for faults as it rolls off. It's a rhythm, and after seven years I can spot a missed pick, that's a gap in the weave, from across the shed. My nan worked in this same mill for thirty years, on the old shuttle looms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the rest of your life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Michael, he works at his dad's garage, and we're getting married next summer at the chapel where I was christened. We rent a little house two streets from my parents. Sundays are church and then dinner at Mum's. I don't use any AI things, I don't even like the self-checkout at the supermarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that people got carried away. Good work still needs good people. I'd say it after church to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the mill carries on and so does my plan. Wedding next summer, maybe a mortgage after. That's all I want, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep my looms running, keep saving about a hundred and fifty a month for the wedding and the house, and help Mum with the flowers for the chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like it's all as it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at the mill you think AI might change even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new fault camera on loom three, I suppose. It spots flaws before I do, sometimes. But someone still has to fix them, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing big changes, what would you want people to understand about your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that people stop treating factory work as something you do if you're not clever. I chose this. My nan was proud of it, and so am I.

S0.say: I'd say I'm glad people got carried away and that good work still needs good people. I'd say it after church to anyone who asked.
S0.think: It means the mill carries on and so does my plan: the wedding next summer and maybe a mortgage after. That's all I really want.
S0.do: Keeps running her looms as normal and saves about 150 a month toward the wedding and a house. Helps her mother with flowers for the chapel.
S0.feel: Calm, as if everything is as it should be.
S0.quote: I chose this. My nan was proud of it, and so am I.
S0.fieldNote: Freya's identity is tied to the mill, her family's history there and her church. She's proud of factory work and wants it respected. She distrusts new technology even at the self-checkout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to stay competitive, and if machines help the mill survive, that's better than it closing. But I'd say they should look after their own people first. Train the ones who've been loyal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared they'd decide one person can watch twelve looms instead of six. That's half of us gone. I'd hope my years there count for something, but I don't know if they would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder, make sure my looms have the fewest faults on the board every week. I'd save a bit more, maybe two hundred a month, and we'd keep the wedding smaller than planned. I wouldn't look for anything new unless the mill asked me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry at the back of my mind on the walk to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you look for new training on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm good at this, not at computers. If the mill wants me to learn the new screens, I'll learn them, they'd show me. But I'm not going to go to college to start from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller wedding look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer guests, maybe sixty instead of a hundred. We'd do the meal in the church hall instead of the hotel. My mum would be disappointed, but she'd understand.

S1.say: I'd say businesses have to stay competitive and machines that keep the mill open beat it closing. But they should look after their loyal people first.
S1.think: I'd be scared they'd have one person watching twelve looms instead of six, which means half of us gone. I'd hope my years count, but I don't know.
S1.do: Works harder to keep the fewest faults on the board and saves about 200 a month. Cuts the wedding to about sixty guests with the meal in the church hall, and waits for the mill to offer training.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a worry at the back of her mind on the walk to work.
S1.quote: I'd be scared they'd decide one person can watch twelve looms instead of six.
S1.fieldNote: Freya accepts the business logic of automation but expects loyalty in return. She'd learn if the mill taught her, but won't seek training herself. The wedding is already being trimmed, which shows the worry is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have put too much faith in machines and not enough in each other. Families and churches will have to hold people up. I wouldn't post it, I'd say it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the mill would be robots within a year and I'd have nothing. If robots do hands-on work too, I don't know what I'd turn to. I'd be frightened, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd bring the wedding forward and make it tiny, just family at the chapel, and save everything else. I'd cut back hard, no new clothes, no going out. If I lost my job, Michael and I would move in with my parents rather than take handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and not sleeping well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather move in with your parents than take handouts. What if government help were offered to everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if there was no other way. But I'd want to work for it if I could, even cleaning or helping at the church. Taking money for nothing doesn't sit right with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Michael's work at the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd still have the garage for a while, I think, but cars that drive themselves don't need much fixing. His dad's been there forty years. It would break his heart before it broke Michael's.

S2.say: I'd say people put too much faith in machines and not enough in each other, so families and churches will have to hold people up. I'd say it at home, not online.
S2.think: The mill would be robots within a year and I'd have nothing to turn to if robots do hands-on work too. I'd be frightened.
S2.do: Brings the wedding forward as a tiny family service at the chapel and cuts all spending on clothes and going out. Moves in with her parents with Michael if she loses her job, rather than relying on government help.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying a lot and sleeping badly.
S2.quote: Taking money for nothing doesn't sit right with me.
S2.fieldNote: Freya's first instinct is family, faith and community rather than the state. She would accept government help only as a last resort. The fast timeline leaves her frightened and with no idea what she'd turn to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the mill to plan and keep its people on, if the bosses care. And I'd say families should start getting ready. I'd keep saying it at home and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd probably have three or four more years at the looms, then the same end. I wouldn't know what to do with the time, if I'm honest. I'd probably just keep going and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding as planned, small, and put off buying a house. I'd save about two hundred and fifty a month. If the mill ran any training for the new machines, I'd sign up, but I wouldn't go looking elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as bad as the fast one. It feels further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had a few years, is there anything else you'd be willing to try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something at church, helping with the old folks' lunch club. That's not a job, though. I'd need the mill to tell me what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep going and hope. Why that, rather than starting something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've never found it easy to start things from nothing. My nan always said, stick at what you know and do it well. I know that might not be enough this time.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for the mill to plan and keep its people if the bosses care, and families should start getting ready. I'd say it at home and at church.
S3.think: I'd probably get three or four more years at the looms before the same end. I wouldn't know what to do with the time, so I'd likely keep going and hope.
S3.do: Keeps the wedding small and puts off buying a house. Saves about 250 a month and joins any training the mill offers without looking elsewhere.
S3.feel: Anxious, though less than the fast picture because it feels further away.
S3.quote: My nan always said, stick at what you know and do it well. I know that might not be enough this time.
S3.fieldNote: More warning eases Freya's alarm but doesn't lead to much action beyond saving and delaying the house. She admits her nan's advice may not fit this future. She looks to the mill and church for direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time for families and communities to look after each other and for people to learn a trade. I'd say apprenticeships are better than handing out money. I'd still say it quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is long enough to have a family and get them settled before it hits. That matters more to me than the job. I'd hope by then there's still some work for people who like working with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned next summer, buy a small house in a few years, and try for children. I'd stay at the mill as long as it needs me, saving about a hundred and fifty a month. If it closed, I'd look at whatever apprenticeships were going, maybe in care with old people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could live with it. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked a lot about family. How does that shape how you'd face this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the fast one, I'd rather lean on family than on handouts. With ten years, I could make sure our family is strong enough to do that. That's how my parents did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to see, growing up in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to see their mum doing an honest day's work. Even if the work changes. That's what my nan gave me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time for families and communities to look after each other and for people to learn a trade, and apprenticeships beat handing out money. I'd say it quietly.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough to have a family and get them settled before it hits, which matters more to me than the job. I'd hope some hands-on work remains.
S4.do: Holds the wedding as planned next summer, plans to buy a small house in a few years and try for children. Stays at the mill as long as needed, saving about 150 a month, and would look at apprenticeships such as care work if it closed.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to live with it, as it's a long way off.
S4.quote: I'd want them to see their mum doing an honest day's work. Even if the work changes.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Freya's attention moves from the job to building her family. She would keep working as long as possible and wait before retraining. Her values of honest work and family support stay consistent throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time to get married properly or settle anything, and I wouldn't know what work to turn to. What would help is the mill training its own people for the new machines, and apprenticeships for real trades, so people can earn their way rather than wait for a cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I think it's right. I don't think it's right to make machines that replace people just because you can. But I don't run the mill, so I'll do my best with what comes.

headlineQuote: I don't think it's right to make machines that replace people just because you can.
portrait: Freya Chen, 27, runs six weaving looms at a textile mill where her nan worked for thirty years, and is engaged to Michael, who works at his father's garage. Church and family are at the centre of her life, and she avoids technology, never using AI. She's calm if AI fizzles, trims her wedding under steady change and is alarmed by AGI in two years, turning to family and church rather than government help. With more time she mostly saves and waits for the mill to guide her, and with ten years she puts building a family first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have no time to marry properly or settle anything and wouldn't know what work to turn to.
whatWouldHelp: The mill training its own people for new machines, and apprenticeships in real trades so people can earn their way.
